utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning ladies and gentlemen. We are back this morning. Mr. Niemann, where will we start now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are ready to proceed, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will have the appearances first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, my name is Niemann, and I appear with my colleagues Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Ms. Van Dusschoten for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: For the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning your Honours, I am Edina Residovic, counsel on behalf of Mr. Zejnil Delalic. My co-counsel is Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, my name is Olujic. I appear on behalf of Mr. Mucic. Regrettably my colleague Michael Greaves is ill today and will not appear in the courtroom today. We wish him a speedy recovery and with your leave your Honours I should like to ask that my assistant Mr. Niko Duric who had been following this trial from the gallery could be with us until Michael Greaves returns. We shall as necessary submit his Procuration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo appearing on behalf of Hazim Delic. My co-counsel is Mr. Thomas Moran from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, my name is John Ackerman and I represent Esad Landzo. My co-counsel is Cynthia McMurray from Houston.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There is nothing coming through on the transcript. What is happening? I think before you commence, we give leave to the assistant of Mr. Olujic to stand in while Mr. Greaves cannot work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to start by making an application, if I may, to interpose a witness by the name of Harraz, who is the next on the list, your Honours. The basis of the application we depose is because -- there is two grounds, firstly the witness himself is anxious to give his evidence today and go, he has other commitments which he has to attend to, but perhaps more importantly, special arrangements have had to be made, your Honour, in respect of interpreters. The witness speaks Arabic and we do not have Arabic interpreters in house and special provision has been made to bring them in. I am informed, your Honours, that the cost of the Arabic interpreters is very very high and they have to be paid in respect of whether or not they are used. They are here today to do this interpreting and if we do not proceed to use them now, we still have to pay the costs -- the Tribunal has to meet the costs of their attendance, which is very extensive. That cost, of course, does not apply for the witness we are seeking to have postponed at the moment, your Honour, so on both those grounds, your Honours, we make this application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will grant leave so that you can change the order and call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us have the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning your Honours. The Prosecution calls Mr. Harraz.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: With respect to the oath, your Honours, and the Registrar, I would advise that this witness does speak some English, so I believe he would be able to take the oath in English, if that would be easiest to have it in his own words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he does speak some English but indicates he would not feel comfortable testifying in full in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly make the interpreter take the oath first. THE INTERPRETER (sworn) ASSA'AD HARRAZ (sworn) Examined by MS. McHENRY

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, may I please ask you to state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Assa'ad Harraz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any nicknames or other names you go by also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Egyptian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your age, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 42 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Journalist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you publish is it always under your name, Mr. Assa'ad Harraz, or do you sometimes use another press name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Assa'ad Taha.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is a name you sometimes use when publishing, is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Taha is my father's name so I am also called Assa'ad Taha.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you in the former Yugoslavia in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were you working for at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was working for several newspapers as a freelance journalist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what languages do you speak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I speak Arabic, a bit of English and a bit of German.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia in 1992, did you have occasion to visit Konjic in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did visit Konjic at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you state when approximately it was that you went to Konjic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify to make sure that I did not have any interpretation error, did you say May, sir, of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I remember, I was there in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain how this trip was arranged, who went on the trip, just a little bit about the logistics of the trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially nothing had been prepared in view of the circumstances prevailing at the time in the region as there was the war on. I went to Split and from Split I met certain friends or certain people who helped us to go to areas of the conflict. We did not intend to go to Konjic in particular, we intended to visit some areas where battles were going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who accompanied you, sir, on this trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was accompanied by some Bosnians, I do not remember their names now. There was also another person that I met and who worked as a cameraman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of this other person and where he was from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ahmed Aamish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where he was from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was Libyan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he was a cameraman, was he a cameraman working for you or was he working on his own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was working alone, but I met him in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he was a cameraman, am I correct in assuming he therefore had some sort of video camera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he has a professional camera, a professional one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you also have an interpreter with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had an Arabic interpreter. I met him in Split, but I would like to rectify something I said in the beginning. I was in Bosnia in May 1992, but in Konjic I was at the end of June or July, I do not remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, with respect to your interpreter, when you say he was an Arabic interpreter, am I correct in assuming that this person could speak Arabic and Serbo-Croatian and he was of Arabic origin, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was an Arab student studying there, so he spoke quite well the local language and, of course, he spoke Arabic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you have a camera with you, not a video camera but just a regular camera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a camera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then Konjic, sir: where did you go on this trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After Konjic I went back to Split and from there went on to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you went to Konjic, did you visit any other areas of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that I went to Mostar and I am not sure whether at that time I visited Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you estimate how long the entire trip took from Split, during the time you were within Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was under a week, perhaps five days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just briefly describe where you went and what you did on this trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived in Konjic in the evening. We met one of the people in charge, Rusim Haji. We spoke with him, we had an interview with him, and then on the next day, we went to the camp. Perhaps there was something else that I do not remember now but after that, at the end of the day, we visited the commander of the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the camp that you went to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I remember that it was a camp for detainees, but I was not given any particular name for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you write any articles setting forth your experiences on this trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and it was published in the Asharq Al-Awsat newspaper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just please briefly tell us with respect to this newspaper where it is published, what language it is published in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a daily newspaper that issued in Arabic from London and it is financed by Saudi financiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long after your trip were the articles published, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think between the beginning of the trip and the publication of the article, between one to two weeks past.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, I would like the witness to be shown -- I would like this to be marked for identification purposes and then shown to the witness, thank you. The Defence has previously been provided copies of these.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is marked as document 167 and the translation 167A. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the article that was published for me in the Asharq Al-Awsat newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can you briefly say what is the subject matter of this article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this article I describe what I have witnessed in this camp in Konjic, approximately the scenes that I have witnessed at that time in that camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what is the date that the article was published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The article was published on Friday, 24th July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now I would like to show you another exhibit, with the assistance of the usher. These have previously been provided to Defence counsel. Sir, you are now being shown what has been marked for identification purposes as Prosecution Exhibit 168. I ask if you can look at that, recognise it and if so, please tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this article, which was published on Saturday 25th July 1992, I speak about the fighting unit that was in that area and a meeting or an interview that I carried with the commander of the area, Zejnil Din.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are these two exhibits your own copies of the published articles; in other words the original from the actual newspaper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these are the copies that I have kept for myself after the publishing of the newspaper that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review the articles immediately after they were published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have read them and I feel that the general gist is compatible with what I have sent. I did not check word for word, but on the whole, the information is what I have sent to the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the information you sent to the newspaper a fair and accurate reflection of your experiences in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I always wanted to ascertain that this is what I have seen, regardless whether that was the reality or not, but this is what I have witnessed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, some pictures are contained in both these exhibits. Can you tell us who took these photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have taken the photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still have the negatives from this trip, the negatives for the photographs or for any additional photographs that were not published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because of my permanent travel from one area to another, I believe I have lost the negatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have to your knowledge any additional photographs that were not published in your possession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have said, unfortunately because of my permanent travel over the last few years, I do not believe that I have any other or additional pictures that would be of any help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you still have any of your notes from this trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not kept them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, am I correct that several names are contained in your articles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there are names of the people or the commanders that I have met.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether or not you are able now to state exactly what these -- how these names would be pronounced in Serbo-Croatian or how they would be written in a Latin script?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not speak Serbo-Croat myself, therefore I had written those names at the time the way I heard them from the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that the Latin alphabet and the Arabic alphabet are different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, there is a difference in the way the alphabet is written and the way it is pronounced, therefore I had transcribed them the way I had heard them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, to the best of your ability, can you tell us the names of the persons you met with on your trip and their positions, if you know them. I would like to start off with -- you indicated before that you met someone named Mr Rusim Haji?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember two people, Mr Zejnil Din and Mr Rusim Haji and other names I do not remember now. This is in fact a chance for me to remind everyone that this event took place around five years ago, which means it is very difficult for me now to remember every detail, particularly that this visit was not a rare visit for me, it was not an event of an unique nature. For it to be outstanding in my memory, it was part of many such visits that I have carried out over many years and in many areas in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you sir. I think everyone understands and appreciates that. With respect to Mr Rusim Haji, are you able to say anything about what his position was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The way he was introduced to me and the way I remember it, it was as though he was the political leader of the area. He was the first person I met when we had arrived that evening in that area, as I have mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to Zejnil Din, what was his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The way he was introduced to me, he was the commander of the area, he was the general military commander of the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know who arranged your meeting with Mr Zejnil Din, who set it up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to remember the names of the people, especially that I have never met them since then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know who arranged your visit to the camp with detainees present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr Rusim Haji facilitated that, with the help of others, as I have said, but as I have mentioned, I do not remember the names of the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just clarify, sir; what visit or visits did Mr Rusim Haji help facilitate? One or both; can you just please explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Him being politically responsible of the area, he promised to facilitate the coverage of the events in the area for the media, but the details I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I am just trying to clarify whether or not, if you remember, whether or not Mr Rusim Haji assisted facilitating your meeting with the commander of the area or the camp or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact that evening he promised to provide all the necessary help to facilitate our generalistic visit to the area and he promised us that the following morning we will commence visiting certain areas, and the next morning indeed we did visit the commander and the camp, but I do not remember if I had visited any other area or any other establishment in that area. This is what he had promised us the night before and he did fulfil it the following morning. Thank you. I should also like to clarify that matters at the time were not at all very organised in a way to say that there were hierarchy in the leadership, the leader and lesser leaders; in fact things were disorganised but the assistance was given on an individual or a personal basis more than a hierarchal organisation of a governmental setup.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you informed of that or was that just your impression from what you could observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the impression that I had of the general situation in Bosnia after the beginning of the war, because of the weakness of the Muslim side things were not fully organised, especially that they did not have a military force that would allow them to set up the political hierarchy needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you went to the camp, did you meet anyone who was in charge of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Croatian person was presented to me as being the man responsible for the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the present time, do you remember the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how it is that you remember that the commander was of a Croatian background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is what I remember and I believe this is what I had mentioned in the newspaper, that he was of Croatian origin, especially that I do not remember meeting another Croatian in such a leading position in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going now to your trip to the camp, do you remember who received you when you went to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have mentioned, I was met by this Croatian commander and he had with him three or four other people whom I was told also were responsible for running the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of any of these other persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the group that you met, who was in charge, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, madam, I did not understand. Which group do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry. You indicated that you met the commander and several other people. I am asking whether or not you know among those people who was in charge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I remember is that this Croatian leader or commander was responsible for the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you observe anything about his relationship with the other people who also went around with you in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was obvious that he was in command, he was the leader, he was giving the instructions to others who were with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just briefly describe what you did at the camp and approximately how long your visit lasted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We visited the wards where the detainees were kept, I believe it was probably two wards or more, then we visited a small room where some patients were kept, then I questioned some detainees very briefly, "why were they detained, why did this happen?" During this interview, we were accompanied by the leadership of the camp, whether the Croatian leader or the people who accompanied him, meaning they were with me all the time. The coverage of the camp was between -- from 45 minutes to one hour, it took.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, so your visit to the camp the entire visit took approximately 45 minutes to one hour; did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is what I do remember with great difficulty. I believe it was from 45 minutes to one hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did I also understand you correctly that on the occasions when you talked to a few of the prisoners that the officials from the camp were also present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were by our side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to the articles you wrote, is it possible for you to now remember all the information contained in the article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I read the articles again and I remember, but unfortunately I do not remember any other things that could be useful in this case. This was not an investigation about the camp, the coverage was aimed at describing the general circumstances prevailing in the area at the time, so I just tried to see what things -- how things were going on then. I did not concentrate on the military side or on the situation of the detainees and where they came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, with respect to the Croatian camp commander that you have mentioned, do you now remember his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything that would refresh your recollection, such as the article you wrote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I read the article, I see his name written down, but I do not remember personally now his name. I remember that he was close to Zejnil Din, or rather that he believed in the necessity of an alliance between the Muslims and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, because this witness has testified he cannot now remember everything about his visit, including names, but that he did accurately reflect it in his article at the time, I would ask that Prosecution Exhibit 167, the article containing his account of the visit, be read out loud by the interpreter and then I will have some specific supplementary questions about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do I have your Honour's permission to ask the interpreter to read out loud the account of the visit that this Prosecution Exhibit 167.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can do so.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. If the interpreters could now, please, in English read out the article, the article of 24th July 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Asharq Al-Awsat visits camp at Konjic. 400 Serbian prisoners treated according to international codes. Chetnik gangs massacre Muslims, Assa'ad Taha. Picture on picture, a programme aired by Croatian TV, comprised several interviews with Muslim prisoners who had been released recently within the prisoner exchange process between the two sides. They spoke of the savage torture they had suffered and the effects were clearly seen on the faces and bodies. This programme preoccupied me as I made my way to the Serbian prisoners' concentration camp in Konjic, a city where the Muslim majority, about 50 kilometres from Sarajevo. Would they also be subjected to such brutal torture? A few minutes later we arrived at the place. It was originally a military barracks which had been captured by the Muslims. The huge gate opened and we passed through and escorted by the commander, we made a quick tour of the camp before we entered one of the wards to see a vivid picture and another side of the tragedy resulting from this accursed war. The camp commander, Zdravko Mucic, said there were over 400 prisoners, some of whom had been captured during fierce battles and had revealed the whereabouts of some of their colleagues of the Serbian militias in hiding. Their fate will be decided, he said, when military operations are halted. Even though we have seen most of them actually shooting down our old men and women, we do not beat or torture them or violate human rights. They shall be given a fair trial. We do not wish to be unjust to anyone, despite all the injustices we have suffered. The camp commander, a Croatian but close to the Muslim command, said: Each one of these prisoners carried two weapons given to him by the Serbian command. Fortunately, lists of names proving that fell into our hands. The mere sight of them, he said, pains me deeply. I would like to avenge the blood of the innocent victims, but I have my orders not to use any forms of violence with them and I respect my command. After a brief pause, he said: I pity those people who acceded to their extremist leadership. But, if we were to release them in the morning, they would be fighting us begin in the evening. They have no other objective but to dominate all other people living with them. In this city, they constitute 15.5 per cent of the population, yet their ambition is to dominate it. The commander, of Croatian origin, said that Croatian leadership were currently playing the same role as the Serbian leadership in mobilising their people against the Muslims. This will involve the Croatian people in battles and confusion with the Muslims. However, I decided to end the conversation there as I was anxious to complete my mission. We started at a medium sized room which, I was told, was the medical clinic for treating prisoners. It contained seven beds occupied by seven prisoners. The beds and woolen blankets looked very clean. To the left there were medicines on the table before which sat a captured Serbian doctor. It appeared that all the wounds were slight. I spoke to one of them and he said: My name is Risto Mrkajic from Bradina. I was hit by a bullet while sitting in my house. I surrendered to the Muslim forces when I realised that I had gone astray. I did not personally hear, nor did I learn from friends and relatives, of the massacre of Muslims in my area. However, I heard on the radio and saw on TV from Foca news of these massacres. Another one said: I surrendered after I became convinced of the deviations and wrongdoings of my commanders. I realised that Muslims were right and for their sake I opposed my Serbian relatives and brothers and began shooting at them. Why are you here then, I asked. But he kept silent. After hearing such movie like (dramatic) answers, I decided I should go to another ward. It was larger than the first. Prisoners sat leaning against the four walls with two other lines sitting in the middle. This ward also appeared very clean. I quickly scanned the faces before me, but I did not see any traces of torture or beating. At least this is what I saw. I spoke to several other prisoners and their answers fell into two main groups. The first group, which refused to abandon the narrow minded nationalistic views that had triggered the war, gave very ambiguous answers to my question. The second group, which sought to escape punishment at any price, was willing to express regret and heap condemnation on the Serbian leadership in Belgrade. In any case, it was obvious that the Serbian prisoners were allowed a large degree of freedom of speech. For example (Midinic) from Bradina, believed that the problem was due to the failure of his command to inform them that Muslim forces had issued a warning, following which the city was attacked. As a result of conflicting orders, the city fell into Muslim hands. He went on to say: We did not really have the desire to fight our Muslim and Croatian brothers... but the command hid many things from us. When I asked him: were the massacres of innocent victims hidden from you, he replied: I never knew that massacres were being perpetrated. I asked his fellow prisoner Georgi Jiberko: Do you consider Bosnia an independent republic or part of Serbia? He hung his head and looked at the floor, saying: some countries have recognised it as an independent republic. Turning to Klimenta Jelko sitting in the opposite row, I asked: have you heard of any incident of rape committed by Muslims against Serbian women? He replied: No, we have never heard of Muslims committing rape. On the contrary, I heard of the mass rape of Muslim women in Bjile. Between the questions and answers, I noticed that the camp commanders were making tremendous effort to control their anger. From time to time they whispered in my ears: This one killed a Muslim... That one is a murderer... This one has committed rape. It was indeed a highly dramatic and tragic situation. The two parties in this camp had one day been school and work mates and there were cases of intermarriage. They shared many stories of human interest as well as memoirs of festivals and burials. How could this suddenly turn into a fire that consumed all? This is what I asked another prisoner, who said: I think that in my area at least all the Serbs blindly followed their leaders who tried to involve the largest number of people in the war. The Serbian Army and party, he continued, armed every one of our people in Bosnia, even in this area, which was impossible to dominate, since we constituted only 13 per cent of the population. But it was necessary for wars to break out and volcanoes of anger to erupt. I asked another if he thought that Muslim prisoners captured by the Serbs were receiving the same treatment that Serbian prisoners were getting here. He said: The treatment here is good and we have no complaints. But I do not know what it is like in the Serbian concentration camps. I heard it was brutal and that there were some cases of murder. The cell block for hard cases. Following this heated session, I decided to walk. But the camp commander said: Wait a minute. I shall drive you to the cell block reserved for dangerous hard cases where you will meet one of the Chetnik leaders. These armed gangs were first formed in 1940 and perpetrated the most brutal and vicious attack against Muslims and Croats alike. It is common knowledge that if they entered a village they would leave nothing alive...They killed every man, beast, plant or bird, and even burnt down houses and they did exactly that in the present war. They brought the prisoner for us to see. His name was Rajko Krjig and he scowled as he came out. I looked at his hands to make sure he was not carrying a weapon. Introducing him, the camp commander said: this man was responsible for cutting off the road between Mostar and Sarajevo and also for the distribution of arms. The man however, said: I had no knowledge of the arms distribution. It was done outside the scope of my authority and in co-ordination with the Serbian party to which I do not belong. I asked: But why were you carrying weapons? I was a former officer, he said, so I took my place on the Crisis Committee to defend the city. To defend it against whom? I asked. To defend our area...we had no aim to attack anyone, he said. To defend against whom, I repeated? This is a very large issue, he said, that involves military and political aspects. In any case, we are linked by neighbourly relations... Here he was loudly interrupted by everyone: The camp commander, the guards, the escort and the translator, all of them vehemently asking about the kind of neighbourliness that allowed for the massacre of neighbours. The commander then posed the question: Who gave you the right to cut off the Mostar Sarajevo road? No one had that right, he replied. How did Serbia help you do that, asked the commander. The man replied very coldly: We blame the Serbian leadership for not giving us the necessary assistance. I then concluded it was time to end the conversation. We will however continue with our story because the military command of the neighbouring area had agreed to help us reach the front lines with the Serbs... but it will be in another despatch.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, in the article you talk about three different areas where prisoners were kept, the ward for sick persons, the very large room and the cell for hard cases; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself go into each of these three different areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the barracks or the ward where the detainees were held and I went to the place where the patients were kept, and then I went to the entrance to the gate of another room where hard cases were kept. I did not go in, but a man was taken out and I mentioned him in the article, from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you not also go into the area reserved for hard cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you estimate, sir, how long you stayed in the area where sick prisoners were kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there very briefly, I do not remember exactly. It was for a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember anything about how the prisoners -- about the atmosphere in this particular ward as compared to the other ward you went to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean the camp or the area of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean: did you notice anything about the atmosphere in the area where sick prisoners were kept as opposed to the atmosphere in the large ward where other detainees were kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the difference between the room where the detainees were kept and the room where the sick people were kept?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the room where the sick people were kept, it was different, it was a small room, and the sick people were on beds, whereas in the other bigger room for detainees, they were sitting on the floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did one or other of these areas seem noticeably more tense or more relaxed or more serious or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The general atmosphere was fine, but, of course, it was a camp where people were not free. But the general impression that a visitor would have to that camp was not that it was a place where torture was being done, but that was a general impression that was given very quickly. Of course, the persons in charge of the camp knew that we were coming on the next day to visit the camp. However, I would like to say once again that the general atmosphere that one could feel there was not an atmosphere of great stress and tension.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were in the camp, sir, did you personally observe any mistreatment of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, your article reports that in the large ward, you quickly scanned the faces of the prisoners and did not see any evidence of torture and mistreatment, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to observe the prisoners closely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as I mentioned, I went into the various rooms and as I said, each ward was big where the detainees were sitting by the walls and in some wards they were sitting also in the middle of the rooms. There were no beds, they were sitting on the floor and as I said, it was a quick visit and I was able to ask some questions to some detainees and then I immediately left the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe any injuries on any prisoners while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps there were two or three who had very slight injuries with little bandages or plaster, but, of course, one should remember that it was a battle area and as I understood, some people were detained or were arrested during the fighting and others were taken from their own neighbourhoods, either they gave themselves in or they were arrested from their area of residence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the prisoners you saw with bandages or plaster or other things, do you have any specific information on how the prisoners received those injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have any particular information, but the impression I got then was that they were a result of the fighting that happened before they were arrested, and I repeat once again, that is what I saw. I can only say that was what I saw or what I was told, I do not know exactly what was happening then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now ask that Prosecution Exhibit 167 be placed under the ELMO with the assistance of the usher. The original of 167, that is the article of July 24th. Sir, can you just please identify by pointing and actually point on the machine, not on the screen in front of you, what the pictures you took are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ones to the left --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to ask that you actually point on that one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The picture to the left is a picture of one of the wards where, as I said, the detainees or prisoners were sitting on the floor. Then in the bottom there is the room where the sick people were kept. The picture after that is the picture of one of the detainees. I do not remember exactly, but perhaps that was the man who was taken out of the room or the cell for hard cases. On the top, there is a picture of one of the commanders in the camp during his talk with the detainee, and then at the bottom, a military truck in a different area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, with respect to the picture above with one of the camp commanders, do you now remember whether or not that is the Croatian camp commander you have testified to, or one of the other commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember if he was the Croat leader, but he was one of the persons in charge of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I would now ask that Prosecution Exhibit 167 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are there any views on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to make a brief comment. I think ordinarily such a newspaper article would not be admissible. It is completely hearsay. I think under the circumstances here today, this witness has basically used it to refresh his recollection which would be the appropriate way for it to be used. However, I have no specific objection to this particular exhibit. I do not want, however, to waive any future objection to any other newspaper article that the Prosecution might want to drag in here, so I just want to say that basically by keeping silent, I am not instituting a waiver process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection, but as a former journalist, I suspect this gentleman would like to keep his originals. I would have no objection to substituting photocopies for the original if that is what the -- if the witness would like to keep the originals.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would join the remarks made by my friend Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we fully subscribe to what has been said by our learned colleague Mr. Ackerman. We, of course, agree that the witness, if he so wants, keeps the original and that we should collate the photostated copy with the original for our purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Exhibit 167 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. If it is the case that we are going to substitute the photocopies, I would just ask that both the Defence counsel and your Honours be permitted to view the original to determine whether or not you think the quality of the photos is better in one such that we should keep the original or should not. The witness has indicated he is willing to provide the court with the originals, although if it is not necessary, he would prefer to give it back, so I would ask just with the usher's assistance that the original be shown to Defence counsel and your Honours for your determination. Going forward now, sir, after your visit to the camp -- sir, after your visit to the camp, did you go anywhere else that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the camp in the evening of that day or at night, we met the commander between two visits. I do not remember up to now if I actually went to another area, but as far as I remember, the visit of the camp took place early in the day and then later there was a visit to the commander of the area. One should take into consideration the distances between areas and the time needed to wait for the preparation of visits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that Mr. Zejnil Din was the commander of the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was introduced to us that way by the people who accompanied us and who was responsible in general for the area. We were told he was the commander of the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it also before you had gone actually to the area, when you were meeting with the Mr. Rusim Haji or anyone else in Konjic, had you also been told anything about the position of Mr. Zejnil Din?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the evening of the first day when we met Mr. Rusim Haji, he promised us to help us meet the general commander of the area, Mr. Zejnil Din and his escorts also the next day promised us the same thing, and the next day, indeed, we went to visit the commander and when we went up to him in a high area he was at a table and on top of it there was written "General commander of the area".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how long was your meeting with the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was no more than half a hour, because we were in a hurry to go back before night would fall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn anything about this person's background, where he lived before the war or what kind of military background he had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was introduced to us, or what they told us at the time, I was a businessman living in Germany, but after the outbreak of the war he left Germany and came to Bosnia to take part in the Defence of areas where Muslims lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I would direct your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 168 and ask if you recognise the picture of the commander and if so, if you would point out that picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the picture in the middle is the picture of the commander and next to it there is the tent which was in that very same place, and it had some communications equipment. Then there is a picture of some of the fighters, but I do not remember if it was taken at the same site where we visited the commander or whether it was taken in another site. As for those flags, I think that picture was taken in another place, not in the place where we met with the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I would now move Prosecution Exhibit 168 into evidence. Any observations on 168?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. This seems to be being offered just for the one photograph that is contained on it and not the language contained within it, since it has not been read to us or referred to in any manner, so I think I would object to the admission of anything but the photographic portion of it. In addition, just as a possible aid, if we are going to give the originals of these back to this gentleman, it occurs to me that our audio visual department may be able to make copies of the photographs appearing on here that are much better than what we are able to accomplish with a copy machine. Just looking at what is showing up on the ELMO, it is better than the xerox machine copies that we have. Maybe that is the way to accomplish both of these tasks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I should like to subscribe to the arguments presented here by my colleague Ackerman. I believe that as far as this article is concerned, we are in no situation to admit it as evidence of the Prosecution because this photograph cannot be the basis for admitting the whole article. At all events, he believe that this decision can be only taken after cross-examination by the Defence counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not have any objection just to admitting it for purposes of the photograph because Defence counsel is correct, that is the main reason for which we seek to introduce it. I believe any other relevant information contained in the article has already been testified to by the witness as being part of his independent recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as this article is concerned, we are in principle against admitting articles as part of the file, but however not even this photograph presented by the Prosecution is not of such significance as to be used for the necessary identification, so, having said this, we are against it because the witness has not stated his views as to the contents of the article, so we feel that it should not be admitted until all the circumstances have been clarified by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, you only want the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour, so we are happy to admit it for purposes of that photograph only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Since there is no objection to the photograph, it is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, where did you go after your meeting with the general commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went back to Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving forward a bit, Mr. Harraz, after your trip to Konjic and other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you have an opportunity to observe the documentary prepared by your colleague, Mr. Aamish, I believe the cameraman originally from Libya?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did see it at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see all the footage taken by Mr. Aamish or just what became part of the final documentary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the final film at the time, as I said, but I did not see all the footage that he took.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of any of the film taken by Mr. Aymish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes our examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examinations?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. We will proceed in this order. First counsel for Mr. Landzo, second counsel for Mr. Delalic, third counsel for Mr. Mucic and fourth counsel for Mr. Delic. Cross-examined by MR. ACKERMAN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. Mr. Harraz, my name is John Ackerman, I represent an accused in this case by the name of Esad Landzo. I take it that is a name that is not familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, that is a name I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The questions I am going to ask you will be brief and I think simple, and I suspect they can be answered with a simple yes. If you would like to clarify your answer to any extent, you can advise me and you may do that, but I will try to keep them as simple as possible. I take it first of all that you have no relationship with an organisation in Belgrade by the name of the Association of Detainees, and that you were not sent here by that association or briefed by that association before you came here, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have no relation with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me now then direct your attention to the time that you visited the Celebici camp, the detention camp that you have been talking about. I think you have told us that your best memory is that that would have been in late June, maybe early July, of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I remember, but with great difficulty and I am not sure of the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You know that it was within probably two weeks before the article was published in the newspaper; that helps you get close at least, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the time that passed between the visit and the publication was about two weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have no reason to come before this Tribunal and attempt to mislead or misdirect this court in any degree, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course not. I came here to say what I saw, whether it would be for the benefit of this party or the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the buildings that you visited while you were at this detention facility was what was a medical facility, a little hospital, so to speak, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a room in the camp that was especially for sick people. There were patients sleeping or lying on beds and there were some medicines there for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the room itself was clean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The beds appeared clean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I saw in general was that the conditions were good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw medicines there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw some medicines there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw a doctor there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember that, but when I read the article I remembered that there was a Serb doctor who seemed to be from the camp also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just observing the patients that you saw in that room on that day, you would not have been able to conclude that any of them were victims of beatings or tortures apart from what wounds they might have received in actual fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I remember, and I am sorry to keep repeating "what I remember", but the events took place five years ago so what I remember is they were sick people, they were not injured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also visited a much larger detention area, the one that is in the photograph that you took where there were a number of people seated on the floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that building appear to you to be clean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any noxious odours in that building that you noticed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not notice anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all of the prisoners that you saw in that building sitting up on the floor, or were some lying around moaning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they looked exactly as they seem in the picture in the article.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anyone in that building for the time that you were in there that you could conclude had been subjected to beatings or torture, from what you could observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked to some of the prisoners at that location, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At least one of those prisoners that you talked to told you that the treatment there was very good and that he had no complaints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you or the cameraman or anyone that was with you while you were there beat or torture any of the prisoners yourselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We were on a journalistic mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I told you that there has been testimony in this case that you and your colleagues engaged in the beating of prisoners, would you say that that is absolutely untrue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also went, did you not, to an area that they told you was a detention facility for what was referred to as the hard cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not a special camp, but a room within the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us that one of those prisoners was brought outside and you observed that particular individual.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was taken out of the room and we talked to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your observations of that particular individual, did you see any indication that that person had been mistreated, beaten, tortured in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was nothing on the outside that could give that impression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let me go just to one other brief area. Also during that trip, you visited the city of Mostar, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that I visited Mostar before going to Konjic, that is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I think it was in Mostar, at least according to your writings, that you visited some members of the Bosnian army, Muslim soldiers, and talked with some of the soldiers, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember now what happened in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. During any part then of your visit to Konjic or the detention camp at Konjic, did you see anything that made you feel like prisoners were being mistreated in a way that you should report it to some kind of an international humanitarian organisation or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the contrary, as I said in the article that was published, I did not see any signs of cruel treatment or mistreatment of the detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it you did not see any evidence by looking at any of the detainees that they were being subjected to starvation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They appeared to be well-fed, as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot judge, but what I saw -- at the end of the visit they were bringing in some food to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it you have seen photographs from some of the Serb camps in that area where the prisoners looked extremely emaciated, clearly had been starved, very much like survivors of the German concentration camps during the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that in the media, not with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: you did not see any prisoners at Celebici that looked like that, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is all I have. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we will have a break now and come back at 12.00. (11.30 am) (A short break) (12.05 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly remind him he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Harraz, I remind you you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, you may proceed. Cross-examined by MS. RESIDOVIC

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Mr. Harraz, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thank you. I shall greet you in your way. Salam Aleikum, Mr. Harraz. Mr. Harraz, you have testified before this court that in July 1992, you visited the region of the commune of Konjic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the translation is not coming through to the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The interpretation is not coming through, I hear, is it. Thank you very much. Can you start all over again?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I should like first of all to introduce myself to you, Mr. Harraz. I am Edina Residovic, I am counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Mr. Harraz, you have testified before this court that in July of 1992, you visited the area of the commune of Konjic, and that after that you wrote a number of articles; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Harraz, in connection with that visit, you wrote three articles; is that so, which were published on 24th, 25th and 26th July; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is so. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition, Mr. Harraz, on 7th March this year, you made a statement to Ms. Sabine Manke, investigator for the Prosecution of the International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have also testified, Mr. Harraz, for the sake of this testimony also you reminded yourself subsequently of what you had written in those articles in 1992; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hence I should like to ask you, Mr. Harraz, since my questions will be linked to your articles, to have these articles before you so as to be able to refresh your memory in connection with my questions. Mr. Harraz, is it true that in those articles -- in the statement made to Ms. Sabine Manke as well as today before the Tribunal, you said that a portion of what you have written in your articles was the result of your direct insight into things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not my viewpoint, it is what I have seen and witnessed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, my next question was precisely to be one to which you have already provided an answer, so you have seen things, you saw some things and you learned about other facts from third persons; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, some of what I had written is what I have witnessed myself, but there might be some information that was given to me by the people that were with the commander or that escorted us that I might have mentioned also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Harraz, you only spent a short time in Konjic and you had no occasion to verify for yourself things which you were told by other persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My mission was not to verify facts, my mission was to describe the general situation in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely in view of the nature of your mission, you did not seek, nor did you see any documentation in the Konjic municipality; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see any documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Harraz, you have also testified before this court that you had an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is because you do not speak the Bosnian language; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with the exception of "dobro dan"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just like my Arabic. Mr. Harraz can you then agree with me that what you found out on the basis of accounts of third persons largely depended also on the precision of the interpretation in regard to the things that were being discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, the interpreter may have a positive or a negative role in conveying the reality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your articles are a general picture, and your impression of what you had seen at that time in the area of the commune of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is correct, and to confirm that, I did mention that in the article; that is to say that I mentioned "this is what I have witnessed as a first view of this site".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the true position of certain persons, you also relied upon the information which was provided to you by third persons; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the leadership that was present in the area by way of escorts and other responsible people who provided us with information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is probably the reason, Mr. Harraz, why, in your articles and in what you have stated before this Tribunal today, there appears some -- in fact, some significant differences in designating the functions of various individuals; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to give me an example?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your article, Mr. Harraz, this gentleman Rusmir, I believe, that is the gentleman in question, although I am not quite sure what you name him, you call him in your article the mayor; then in your third article you say that you had paid a visit to the war presidency where you conducted a conversation. In your statement to Miss Sabine Manke, you said that the local governor had been in question, and today as far as I could gather, you said that he was the political leader of the area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. This person might include all these posts, but as I have mentioned before, there was no evident hierarchical division and these titles are the titles that were given to me at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this example which I have used of Mr. Rusmir, is it not that it is in the same way that you learned about the other time that you met in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I referred to the post and the responsibility in accordance with the information that was given to me, in accordance to what was said to me in the area and not by the leadership in Sarajevo, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr Harraz, are you aware of the fact that it was precisely at that time that there was a certain Arabic organisation in Konjic which was engaged in humanitarian aid, the objective of which was to find out facts which would be of assistance in collecting such aid and relief supplies for the suffering population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina in general there were Arab relief agencies, many of them, but in Konjic in particular I do not remember if there was any such agency at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Harraz, was it one of the intentions of your account of the situation in Konjic to acquaint the Arabic public better with the difficult circumstances in this region and to bolster efforts in providing humanitarian relief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a journalistic mission in my capacity as a journalist to give the Arab population a viewpoint on what is happening in that part of the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Harraz, is that the reason why you perhaps in a certain way placed more stress on the option of this people towards Islam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to rephrase your question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will start with another question. In that area, Mr. Harraz, you did not meet any people who were fanatical Islamists, who were committed to hatred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe that in Bosnia at that time there were people or fanatic trends; in fact the Muslims were very far from their religion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Irrespective of the fact that they had suffered very much prior to your visit, amongst the fighters you did not feel that they needed to retaliate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, what I felt was that there was a great desire to defend their area, and they truly believed that they had no other option but to defend their area because they have nowhere else to go or no other party that can come to their aid. The general feeling that I had was they had to defend themselves in order to defend the areas in which they live.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Harraz, you said that in the evening you visited Mr. Hadzihuseinovic. Is it true that Mr. Hadzihuseinovic gave you data regarding the structure of the population, the aggression and the current military situation in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information that was given to me -- as I said, he was the governor of the city, or it can be explained as the military governor. Added to that he had political responsibilities and in that capacity we interviewed him at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Hadzihuseinovic also told you that there were very many refugees who had arrived to Konjic at that time from the areas which were under temporary occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did speak of the humanitarian situation and the situation of the refugees, but I do not remember details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Mr. Harraz, you probably recall that he told you that at that time, the humanitarian situation, the supply of the population and the refugees was very difficult indeed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did mention that and it was a known fact to everyone, not just to people in Konjic but in other regions of Bosnia as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have testified before this Tribunal that you had learned that hierarchy was not quite clear in the governmental set-up, and that you found out these things on the basis of your general knowledge about Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that at the time, this hierarchical set-up was not there and every region, one way or another, took care of defending their borders or the internal affairs but, of course, there was some kind of communication between the area, but the general remark is that there was no clear administrative structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thank you for your opinion generally about the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but can you confirm that after all, you did not thoroughly perceive the situation in the sense of the organisation of authority in the commune of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, of course not. This was not my mission, and I repeat that I spent a relatively short time in the area, and I did describe what was said to me and what I had witnessed. I did not seek to verify the information because this kind of media or articles does not aim at providing evidence but to describe events in a certain area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So although you talked to the mayor during that conversation, in the course of your stay you did find out that the town of Konjic in which authority structures did function in a certain way, was handicapped by various blockades mounted by Serbian forces, by the Serbian forces but already at that time also by the Croatians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I remember is that they were subject to an attack by the Serbs. As for the Croatian side, I believe that at the time matters were still relatively quiet between the two parties; that is between Muslims and Croats, at least on the outside, in a general outlook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Harraz, I am actually -- I actually want to ask you questions so that things could be clear for us all here. I believe that it is very important that you as a witness of that period should be before this court, because the number of persons as courageous as you were who decided to go to Bosnia in those times is really small. I believe that because of this you will understand the nature of the question which I am about to ask you. You have just said that you have witnessed the shelling and the bombardment of Konjic from Serbian positions; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the area was subject to shelling by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your short stay you could see vast destruction to housing and other structures throughout the city; is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Konjic did have many areas that were destroyed, as well as the destruction in many other areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Harraz, you described in some more detail in the article which was published on July 24th 1992 which was also read before this court, therefore in connection with this article I should only like to ask you a few questions. You entered and you saw a room which was the infirmary, the sick ward.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the room where the sick people were?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What you have written in your article of 27th is the result of what you personally saw.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You came in and you saw this hangar, this large room in which there were many prisoners; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you have written in your article about how this room looked, how the prisoners looked and about the conditions which prevailed in the room is also the result of what you saw for yourself; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, I wrote that on the basis of what I saw myself, not on the basis of what anybody else told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The photograph which has been shown before this court which you said you thought depicted the person which you think was the organiser, who was taken out from that special cell for the dangerous, is the person of whom you personally took a photograph; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said this morning that this man -- I gathered that he was in that hard cell block, but I cannot be sure that this is the person that we see in the picture, that he was the man in the hard cell block.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person was taken out of that room; if I remind you, if I could refresh your memory, is Rajko Dordic, the man who was known as the organiser of the Defence of Bradina and of the arming of Serbs; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information that I put down in the article is based on what I was told about the man, the man who was taken out of that special place, but I repeat that I am not sure whether this is the picture of that man, the picture that is in the article.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not asking you about the photograph, Mr. Harraz, but about the talk which you had with the man which you referred to in your article.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information in the article is the information given to me and the talk in the article is the talk that went on between me and the man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you witnessed the fact that he was told in your presence that he was responsible for cutting off the Mostar/Sarajevo road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also witnessed his reply, namely that he was dissatisfied with the assistance which the leadership of Serbia had extended to them to aid their resistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
